The Story of Vidyuchchar Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the bestower of all happiness and counted as supreme in the world, and I write the story of Vidyuchchar Muni according to the scriptures.

In the kingdom of King Vamarath of Mithilapur, a man named Yamdand was appointed as the chief of police. In the same city lived a thief named Vidyuchchar. He was very skilled in his trade of thievery. His method was this: during the day, he would disguise himself as a leper and stay in a deserted temple. As soon as night fell, he would take the form of a handsome man and enjoy himself to his heart's content. This trick had been working for many days, and no one could recognise him.

One day, Vidyuchchar stole the king's own jewel necklace right before his eyes. The king could do nothing about it at the time. In the morning, the king summoned the chief of police and said, "Look, some thief, with his handsome disguise, has enchanted me and taken my jewel necklace. Therefore I order you to present that necklace or the thief who stole it before me within seven days, or you shall face the full punishment. It seems you are very negligent in your duty. Otherwise, how can a theft occur in the royal palace? It is no small matter."

Saying "As you command," the chief of police set out to find the thief. He searched every lane, alley, and house in the city but found no trace of the thief. Six days passed this way. On the seventh day, he went out again. Walking along, his eye fell on a deserted temple. He went inside and found a leper lying there. Seeing the leper's appearance, the chief of police became suspicious. He engaged him in conversation in such a way as to probe his mind. Though the conversation did not yield the success he wanted, it confirmed his initial suspicion. The chief of police brought the leper before the king and said, "Maharaj, this is the thief of your necklace."

When questioned, the leper flatly denied being a thief, saying, "I am not a thief. They have forcibly brought me here." The king looked at the chief of police. The chief still insisted firmly, "Maharaj, this is the thief. There is no doubt." Seeing the chief of police make such a claim without any proof, the king ordered a test. He had the leper and several other suspects brought forward and subjected them to various examinations. Through these tests, Vidyuchchar's true identity was revealed. He was caught and punished, and the necklace was recovered.

After this life, Vidyuchchar, through the ripening of merit, was reborn as a monk named Vidyuchchar. He practised intense austerities and meditation, destroyed his karmas, and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that no crime, no matter how cleverly concealed, can remain hidden forever. Vidyuchchar's disguise as a leper fooled many, but the chief of police's keen observation and the king's wise tests eventually uncovered the truth. The wise should understand that all actions, good or bad, bear fruit in due time. Those who commit sins may escape detection in this life, but they cannot escape the consequences in future lives. True wisdom lies in practising dharma and avoiding all forms of wrongdoing.
